title: Using the MQL5 Economic Calendar for News Filter (Part 5): The Tier the Calendar Does Not Have
text:
Contents
Introduction
Scope of This Article
Two Copies of One Decision
Section 1: The Vocabulary
Section 2: The Rules
Section 3: The EA
Reading Your Own Broker
What This Part Does Not Do
Conclusion
Introduction
The news filter we have built so far in
Part 4
of this series reads the broker's economic calendar, works out which events touch the chart symbol, blocks new trades inside a window around them, suspends and restores stops, survives a terminal restart, and runs all of it against a static CSV file when the Strategy Tester is driving. Every event the calendar tags as "High" gets the same treatment. For most high-impact releases, that is what you want. You set a window on either side, the EA stands down for that long, and the release passes.
A few releases behave differently. A central bank rate decision, the statement published with it, and the press conference that follows do not simply move price; they can change where the market thinks policy is going. Price can then keep adjusting for longer than the window you would give a routine release. A regional manufacturing survey can spike the chart just as hard and be fully absorbed inside two minutes. The calendar tags both of them "High," and this part does not dispute the tag. Importance is one question, and the tag answers it. How much room a release needs is a second question, which the tag was never meant to answer: it does not separate the kind of release that can reset expectations from the kind that is absorbed before the next bar closes. Whether a particular release did reset them is known only after it is out, and this part does not try to measure that. It works one step earlier: you decide in advance which kinds of release get more room, and the filter gives that room to every release a rule names.
What this can cost depends on the strategy, its settings, and the instrument. Three examples:
A mean-reversion system can take the other side of the spike and wait for a return to a mean that has moved.
A trend system can be whipsawed out on the first leg and then watch the real move happen without it.
A system with a fixed stop can meet a market moving faster than the distance that stop was sized for.
You need a way to mark a specific release as different and have the filter treat it differently, without giving up the calendar's tagging for everything else. By the end of this part, the EA will:
Rank events on one ordered scale that keeps the calendar's four importance levels and adds a special tier above them.
Take its list of special releases from a rule table instead of an input; with a CSV file, you can edit to add releases, override the shipped ones, or drop an event you have decided to ignore.
Give every event its own before and after window, so a rate decision holds the filter open longer than a routine release without changing what the routine release gets.
Classify events once, through one function shared by the live calendar and the backtest CSV.
Come with a script that prints what your own broker's calendar publishes so the rules you write match what your terminal reports.
Scope of This Article
This part changes how the EA decides that an event matters. The actions stay the same: it blocks new trades, closes positions before a release, and suspends stops during the window. This part only changes which events trigger those actions and for how long. There are five files:
NewsTypes.mqh
and
NewsRules.mqh,
which go in
MQL5\Include\NewsFilterSuite\
. This is the first time this series has put code in a header instead of in the EA. The reason is specific: a script, or a second EA, will want to read the tier scale and the rule table without depending on the trading system, and the
Reading Your Own Broker
section does exactly that.
NewsIntegration_Part5.mq5
, the EA.
NewsTierInspector.mq5
, a script for
MQL5
\Scripts
\
.
NewsRules.csv
, a sample override file for
Common
\Files\
. Its full text is printed under the
Overriding the Table
subsection.
Two Copies of One Decision
Before adding anything, open
isUpcomingNews()
in your EA and look at what is already there. The tester branch decided on importance like this:
//--- Importance filter
bool
okImportance =
false
;
switch
(NewsImportanceMode)
           {
case
NEWS_HIGH_ONLY:
               okImportance = (historicalNews[i].importance ==
3
);
break
;
case
NEWS_MODERATE_ONLY:
               okImportance = (historicalNews[i].importance ==
2
);
break
;
case
NEWS_HIGH_AND_MODERATE:
               okImportance = (historicalNews[i].importance >=
2
);
break
;
           }
if
(!okImportance)
continue
;
Further down the same function, the live branch decides it again:
//--- Importance Filter
bool
okImportance =
false
;
switch
(NewsImportanceMode)
        {
case
NEWS_HIGH_ONLY:
            okImportance = (ev.importance ==
CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_HIGH
);
break
;
case
NEWS_MODERATE_ONLY:
            okImportance = (ev.importance ==
CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_MODERATE
);
break
;
case
NEWS_HIGH_AND_MODERATE:
            okImportance = (ev.importance ==
CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_HIGH
|| ev.importance ==
CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_MODERATE
);
break
;
        }
if
(!okImportance)
continue
;
The two blocks reach the same answer for a reason that is not enforced anywhere: the tester block tests for the number 3, the live block tests for CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_HIGH, and only the export script, which writes 3 for a high-impact event, connects the two. Change what the file writes, and only one of the two blocks has to follow. While this decision is only a single numeric comparison, maintaining two copies costs almost nothing. The special tier adds more logic: it reads an event name, matches it against a rule table, assigns a tier, and resolves a window.
If implemented twice, you must keep two tables aligned, and the backtest can diverge from the live EA for that reason alone. The first change in this part, therefore, moves the decision into one place that both branches can call. That removes the second copy. It does not make the two sources identical, and the One Classifier subsection lists what else has to hold for them to agree.
Section 1: The Vocabulary
First we create a header file called
NewsTypes.mqh
with the necessary properties. Like this:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//|                                                    NewsTypes.mqh |
//|                                    Copyright 2026, soloharbinger |
//|                      https://www.mql5.com/en/users/soloharbinger |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
#property
copyright
"Copyright 2026, soloharbinger"
#property
link
"https://www.mql5.com/en/users/soloharbinger"
#property
version
"1.00"
#property
description
"Vocabulary for the news filter: the tier scale, one event record, one rule, and the classifier's configuration."
#ifndef
NEWSFILTERSUITE_NEWSTYPES_MQH
#define
NEWSFILTERSUITE_NEWSTYPES_MQH
NewsTypes.mqh
defines the terms the rest of the part is written in: a scale for importance, a record for a classified event, a record for a rule, and the settings the classifier reads. It contains no trading logic and includes nothing.
The Tier Scale
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| The tier scale                                                   |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
enum
ENUM_NEWS_TIER
  {
   NEWS_TIER_NONE     =
0
,
// Untagged by the calendar
NEWS_TIER_LOW      =
1
,
// Calendar: low importance
NEWS_TIER_MODERATE =
2
,
// Calendar: moderate importance
NEWS_TIER_HIGH     =
3
,
// Calendar: high importance
NEWS_TIER_SPECIAL  =
4
// Ours: releases the calendar cannot separate from the rest of High
};
The first four values keep the numbers the historical file already uses in its importance column: 1 for low, 2 for moderate, and 3 for high, with 0 added for an event the calendar leaves untagged. A number read from the file is therefore already on this scale, and
TierFromImportance()
only keeps it inside that range. The calendar's own value is never read as a number. The documentation lists the four names of ENUM_CALENDAR_EVENT_IMPORTANCE and gives them no numeric values, so
ImportanceFromCalendar()
converts by name:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Calendar importance as the 0 to 3 number the historical file     |
//| uses. Converted by name, never by the enum's own value           |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
int
ImportanceFromCalendar(
const
ENUM_CALENDAR_EVENT_IMPORTANCE
importance)
  {
switch
(importance)
     {
case
CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_HIGH
:
return
3
;
case
CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_MODERATE
:
return
2
;
case
CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_LOW
:
return
1
;
default
:
return
0
;
// CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_NONE
}
  }
Nothing in the code now depends on how that enum is numbered. The scale also corrects something from earlier. The calendar publishes four importance levels, not three. CALENDAR_IMPORTANCE_NONE is the fourth, and it is why this scale starts at zero. The numbers in the file remain a convention, as they are in any file format: the script that writes the file and the loader that reads it must agree on them. The export script in
Part 4
writes 1 for an untagged event as well as for a low one, so a file made with it cannot tell the two apart, while the inspector's export writes 0.
Value 4 sits above the calendar's highest rather than beside it, which makes the scale ordered. "Watch this tier and everything above it" then becomes one test, and that is what replaces ENUM_NEWS_IMPORTANCE_MODE. The test is
TierMeetsThreshold()
, which returns tier >= minimum && tier > NEWS_TIER_NONE. Its second condition means an event at tier 0 is never watched, even with
NewsMinimumTier
set to NEWS_TIER_NONE, a setting that watches Low and everything above it. The three old modes were mutually exclusive sets, so asking for more room around rate decisions meant selecting a mode that excluded everything else. With an ordered scale, one input covers both cases:
NewsMinimumTier
= NEWS_TIER_HIGH watches High and Special together, and a special event brings its own wider window with it. Existing settings map across like this:
Old setting
New setting
NEWS_HIGH_ONLY
NewsMinimumTier
= NEWS_TIER_HIGH
NEWS_HIGH_AND_MODERATE
NewsMinimumTier
= NEWS_TIER_MODERATE
NEWS_MODERATE_ONLY
no equivalent
NEWS_MODERATE_ONLY restricted trading on moderate news while trading straight through rate decisions. An ordered scale cannot express that, because everything at or above the threshold is watched. If you were using that mode, this part removes the capability. The ordered scale is therefore a trade and not a pure gain: one threshold and a tier above High, at the price of the one mode that skipped a level.
The Event Record
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| One event, after classification                                  |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
struct
SNewsEvent
  {
datetime
time;
string
currency;
string
name;
string
code;
   ENUM_NEWS_TIER    reportedTier;
// What the source said
ENUM_NEWS_TIER    tier;
// What the rules decided
int
minutesBefore;
// This event's own window, not a global setting
int
minutesAfter;
bool
affectsSymbol;
// Relevance to the chart symbol, decided once at load
int
ruleIndex;
// Rule that classified it, -1 if none matched
};
The EA has described an event with a time, a currency, an importance number, and a name. Those four fields answer whether an event is important. They cannot answer how long the event needs to remain in scope, because there is nowhere to record that.
reportedTier
and
tier
hold the source's answer and the rules' answer separately. Keeping both means the difference can be printed instead of inferred, and it settles what the rule table is: an addition to the calendar's tagging rather than a replacement for it. An event that matches no rule comes out of the classifier exactly as the calendar described it.
minutesBefore
and
minutesAfter
store the window on the event. Previously, the window was read from a global input inside the detection loop, which is why every event received the same treatment. With the window on the record, the detection loop asks each event how much room it wants.
affectsSymbol
and
ruleIndex
are both computed once when events are loaded and then carried with the event, rather than recomputed on every tick. The EA section covers how relevance gets decided.
The Settings the Classifier Reads
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Everything the classifier needs, in one place                    |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
struct
SNewsConfig
  {
//--- What counts as news worth acting on
ENUM_NEWS_TIER    minimumTier;
//--- Windows in minutes. Special events get their own pair
int
defaultBefore;
int
defaultAfter;
int
specialBefore;
int
specialAfter;
//--- Rule table
bool
loadBuiltInRules;
string
rulesFile;
//--- Diagnostics
bool
verbose;
void
SetDefaults(
void
);
  };
There are two window pairs, one threshold, two rule-table settings, and a verbose flag.
SetDefaults()
fills in starting values so a caller overrides only what it cares about. Passing settings in a structure rather than reading inputs directly is what allows a caller with no inputs of its own to classify events. The EA fills this in from its input block. The inspector script fills in the same structure from its own inputs, and both get identical classification.
Section 2: The Rules
NewsRules.mqh
holds the rule table and the classifier that reads it. It includes
NewsTypes.mqh
and nothing else.
A Rule Is Data
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| One rule: which events get moved to which tier, and how much     |
//| room they are given                                              |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
struct
SNewsRule
  {
string
currency;
// Three-letter code, or "*" for any
string
match;
// Stored uppercase, read according to matchMode
ENUM_NEWS_MATCH   matchMode;
   ENUM_NEWS_TIER    tier;
// Tier this event moves to, up or down
int
minutesBefore;
// -1 inherits the configured window for the resulting tier
int
minutesAfter;
// -1 inherits
};
A list of releases that deserve different handling is data. When the list is written as a chain of string comparisons inside the EA, every addition needs a recompile, and finding out what is on the list means reading the program. Written as a table of structures, the list can be loaded from a file, printed, counted, and edited without touching the EA.
currency
accepts * to match any currency, so one rule can cover a release that several central banks publish under the same words, such as an interest rate decision.
minutesBefore
and
minutesAfter
take -1 to mean inherit whatever window the resulting tier is configured with. A rule states a window only when it wants something different from the tier default.
tier
moves an event up the scale or down it, so a rule can take a release out of the filter as easily as it can promote one.
Two Ways to Name an Event
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Does this rule describe this event?                              |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
bool
NewsRule_Matches(
const
SNewsRule &rule,
const
string
upperCurrency,
const
string
upperCode,
const
string
upperName)
  {
if
(rule.currency !=
"*"
&& rule.currency != upperCurrency)
return
false
;
switch
(rule.matchMode)
     {
case
NEWS_MATCH_CODE:
return
(
StringLen
(upperCode) >
0
&& upperCode == rule.match);
case
NEWS_MATCH_EXACT:
return
(upperName == rule.match);
default
:
return
(
StringFind
(upperName, rule.match) != -
1
);
     }
  }
Currency is checked first and rejects the rule immediately if it does not match, which avoids the string comparisons for most rules on most events. Substring matching is the default. It suits releases that appear under a name containing a phrase you can recognize, and it tolerates a broker adding a prefix or a month to the name. Exact matching exists for cases where a substring catches something it should not, and a short phrase catches more. A substring rule written as "Nonfarm" matches "Nonfarm Payrolls" and also "ADP Nonfarm Employment Change," which is a different release published on a different day. That rule would open the special window on both days. The built-in table, therefore, uses exact matching for its short names, because "CPI m/m" as a substring would also match "Core CPI m/m" and every other name that contains it.
Code matching compares against
MqlCalendarEvent.event_code
, which is stored alongside name. The documentation describes name as the event's text in the terminal language, so a name rule works only in the language it was written in. It describes
event_code
only as the event code. It attaches no language to the code, which is the reason to prefer a code rule where names are translated, but it does not promise the same code on every server either. The shipped table therefore matches on names. A name is the field you can check against the calendar already open in front of you, while the codes have to be read off your own terminal first. The script near the end of this article prints them.
The Built-In Table
One question decides what goes on the list: Is this the kind of release that can change where the market thinks policy is going, or the kind that only moves price for a few minutes? The answer is a judgment about a kind of release, made in advance, and not a measurement of any single one. The rate decision of each of the eight central banks is on the list with the communication around it, and so are a few of the inflation and employment numbers that strongly influence those decisions. That gives thirty-four rules across eight major currencies. The list is not complete even by its own question: it has no inflation rule for Japan or Switzerland, for example, and none for the US unemployment rate. Each block looks like this:

//| The built-in table                                               |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+

NewsRules_LoadBuiltIn(
void
)
  {
int
before =
ArraySize
(g_newsRules);
//--- USD
NewsRules_AddSpecial(
"USD"
,
"Fed Interest Rate Decision"
, NEWS_MATCH_NAME);

"USD"

   NewsRules_AddSpecial(

"USD"

NewsRules_AddSpecial()
is shorthand for a rule that moves an event to the special tier and inherits the configured special window, which is what every shipped rule does. One window for all thirty-four is a default, and not a claim that they all need the same room: nothing here measures how long any of them moves the market. A rule can give a single release its own window, as the next subsection shows. Rule names are stored uppercase, and events are uppercased before comparison, so the capitalization you write here is not relevant.
Overriding the Table
The built-in list is a starting position. Your instrument may not care about half of it and may need something that is not on it. NewsRules.csv is how you say so, and its commented header is the configuration reference:
# NewsRules.csv - optional overrides for the built-in special tier table.
#
# Place in the terminal's Common\Files folder. Nothing here is required.
# The built-in table works without this file, and this file only extends
# or overrides it. Rules loaded from here beat built-ins that describe
# the same event, because the classifier walks the table backwards and
# stops at the first match. For the same reason, a later line in this
# file beats an earlier one, whatever its mode. Write broad rules first
# and narrow ones after them.
#
# Columns
#   currency   Three-letter code, or * for any currency
#   match      What to compare against, read according to mode
#   mode       code  = whole MqlCalendarEvent.event_code
#              exact = whole event name
#              name  = substring of the event name
#   tier       0 None  1 Low  2 Moderate  3 High  4 Special
#              Use 0 to drop an event your broker tags high but you ignore
#   before     Minutes before the event. -1 inherits the configured window
#   after      Minutes after the event.  -1 inherits
#
# Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored, as is this header row.
#
currency,match,mode,tier,before,after
#
# --- Per-event windows -------------------------------------------------
# The built-in table gives every special event the same configured
# window. These four ask for more. The minute values below demonstrate
# the mechanism; they are not measured figures. Test on your own
# instrument before trusting any number here.
#
USD,FOMC Press Conference,name,4,20,90
USD,Nonfarm Payrolls,exact,4,30,75
USD,Fed Interest Rate Decision,name,4,20,90
EUR,ECB Monetary Policy Press Conference,name,4,15,75
#
# --- Matching on event_code --------------------------------------------
# A name is shown in the terminal's language, so a name rule works in
# that language only. The code is a separate field with no language
# attached to it. The built-in table does not use codes because the
# strings have to be read off your own terminal first.
# NewsTierInspector.mq5 prints the code beside every event; copy the
# ones you care about into rules like this. A code rule matches on live
# data only, because the historical news file has no code column.
#
# USD,
<paste-the-
code
-here>
,code,4,30,75
#
# --- Demotion ----------------------------------------------------------
# Anything your broker tags high that you have decided does not move your
# instrument. An event at tier 0 is never watched, whatever
# NewsMinimumTier is set to.
#
# USD,EIA Crude Oil Stocks Change,name,0,-1,-1
The file is optional, and the filter runs without it. When the file is missing and verbose is on, the loader prints one line saying that the built-in rules are used alone. That line carries the terminal's code for a file that could not be opened, 5004, as the inspector's output shows later. It is information, and nothing fails. The loader reports how many rules it read and how many lines it rejected. A line is rejected when it has fewer than four columns or an empty currency or match field, and the Experts tab gives its line number. A minute value below -1 is read as -1. Built-in rules load first; file rules append after them; matching walks the table backwards.
A rule from your file, therefore, takes precedence over a built-in rule describing the same event, and you override by adding a line rather than editing the library. The same order applies inside the file. Of two lines that match the same event, the later one wins, whatever their modes, so a broad name rule placed after an exact rule replaces it. Write the broad rules first and the narrow ones after them, then check the rule listing the inspector prints, which shows the mode and tier each rule was read with. Each promoted or demoted line in its event listing also names the rule that decided it, and that is where a rule shadowed by a broader one shows up.
The four sample rules in the file give the FOMC press conference, Nonfarm Payrolls, the Fed rate decision, and the ECB press conference wider windows than the tier default. A rule can also assign tier 0, which drops an event below every threshold. That is how you tell the filter your broker tags a release high and you have decided it does not move your instrument.
Those example minute values used in the news window demonstrate the mechanism. They are not measured; nothing in this suite derives a window from realized volatility, and they should be replaced with numbers you have tested on your own instrument.
One Classifier
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| The classifier                                                   |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
void
NewsRules_Classify(
const
SNewsConfig &cfg,
const
datetime
eventTime,
const
string
currency,
const
string
eventCode,
const
string
eventName,
const
int
reportedImportance,
                        SNewsEvent &event)
  {
   event.time          = eventTime;
   event.currency      = NormalizeField(currency);
   event.name          = eventName;
   event.code          = eventCode;
   event.reportedTier  = TierFromImportance(reportedImportance);
   event.tier          = event.reportedTier;
   event.ruleIndex     = -
1
;
   event.affectsSymbol =
false
;

   NewsRules_ResolveWindow(cfg, event.tier, event.minutesBefore, event.minutesAfter);
string
upperCode = NormalizeField(eventCode);
string
upperName = NormalizeField(eventName);
//--- Backwards, so a rule loaded from file beats a built-in that
//--- describes the same event
for
(
int
i =
ArraySize
(g_newsRules) -
1
; i >=
0
; i--)
     {
if
(!NewsRule_Matches(g_newsRules[i], event.currency, upperCode, upperName))
continue
;

      event.tier      = g_newsRules[i].tier;
      event.ruleIndex = i;

      NewsRules_ResolveWindow(cfg, event.tier, event.minutesBefore, event.minutesAfter);
if
(g_newsRules[i].minutesBefore >=
0
)
         event.minutesBefore = g_newsRules[i].minutesBefore;
if
(g_newsRules[i].minutesAfter >=
0
)
         event.minutesAfter = g_newsRules[i].minutesAfter;
break
;
     }
  }
The function runs in four steps. First, it copies the source fields and converts importance to a tier. Second, it resolves the default window for that tier. Third, it scans the rules table backwards for a match. Fourth, on a match, it updates the tier, resolves the window again, and overrides the window if the rule specifies explicit values. The
break
ends the search at the first match.
Both loaders call this function. The live loader passes
ev.event_code
,
ev.name
, and the importance that
ImportanceFromCalendar()
converts. The CSV loader passes the time, currency, importance, and name it reads from the file and an empty string for the code. The classifier itself cannot differ between the two, because there is only one. That removes one cause of a backtest disagreeing with live trading, and only that one. The two agree when four more things hold: the rules match on names and not on codes, because the file has no event code; the file's names are in the same language as the live terminal's, because names are translated; its times are server times; and it covers the tested period completely, with the importance the calendar gave each event.
When they hold, the same event gets the same tier and window in both. The value of a single implementation grows with the rules. Two switches agreeing on a single numeric comparison are easy to check by reading both. Two rule tables, two sets of matching modes, and two window resolutions are not, and the first symptom of drift would be a backtest trading through a release the live EA refuses. A backtest that disagrees with live trading without showing it can do more harm than no backtest, because it produces confidence instead of a visible gap.
Classification also moves off the tick. The existing EA evaluates event importance on every tick in both branches. Because importance depends only on the event and the rules, it does not change tick-to-tick. It is now settled once when events are loaded and stored on the record and the detection loop reads a decision that has already been made. The threshold is settled at the same moment. A loader stores an event only if
TierMeetsThreshold()
accepts its tier, so the detection loop never meets an event below
NewsMinimumTier
or at tier 0.
Sharing one implementation between a live source and a test source is a common answer to this problem rather than an original one. Other implementations reach the same place by a different route, wrapping the calendar in interchangeable providers so that the live connector and CSV reader expose the same interface to the EA. What is here is narrower: one classifier and two loaders, with no provider abstraction.

Two Loaders, One Array

Both loaders fill it. The raw

The calendar query ran from now forward, which was harmless while the window after a release was a few minutes wide. A special event can hold the filter open for an hour after it fires, and an event that occurred twenty minutes before a reload or restart would not be in the array at all. The query now reaches back by the longest after-window any event can be given. That is the larger of the two inputs, or a rule's own value when a rule sets more, as two of the sample rules do with 90 minutes:

This step, in each loader, is the only place the threshold is applied. An event that fails TierMeetsThreshold() never enters newsEvents[], so the scan shown later has no tier left to test. It is also how a rule that assigns tier 0 takes an event out of the filter: the event is classified, fails the test, and is not stored.
The CSV loader changes less. It reads the same four columns as before. It now accepts an importance of 0 to 3, the calendar's full range, where it used to reject 0. Not only that, it also removes the quotation marks that the
Part 4
export script puts around each name so that an exact rule can match the whole name. The larger change is where a parsed row goes: into the classifier and through the same threshold test, rather than into a separate array with a separate importance test. The file carries no event code, so a code-matching rule cannot fire against historical data. Name and exact rules are applied to the file's names exactly as they are to the calendar's. The loader also looks for the header row only at the start of a line now. The earlier test looked for "time" and "date" anywhere in the line and so dropped every event whose name contains those letters, as "Sentiment" does.

The print at the end is a useful first check. In the tester, where the whole file is loaded, zero relevant events on a major pair usually mean the currency cache did not build, and the filter will remain inactive for the whole run. On a live chart, the count covers only about the next 24 hours, so a zero can also mean a quiet day.

The function is simpler because several decisions moved to load time. The scan has no MQL_TESTER branch, no tier test, and no currency comparison, because the loaders stored only the events that passed
TierMeetsThreshold()
and relevance was marked after they ran. Inside the loop, it only checks the time window and optionally logs the detection. The reload check at the top is the only part that still distinguishes between the two modes, and it governs refreshing the source rather than interpreting it. The symbol argument is kept so that existing calls still compile.
The answer is always for the chart symbol, because relevance was marked for it at load. When a call passes any other symbol, the function says so once in the Experts tab and still answers for the chart symbol, so it cannot serve as a filter for a second instrument. The scan returns at the first event in the array whose window is open, and the log line prints that event's tier and resolved window. When two windows overlap, as those of a rate decision and its press conference can, the line names the first of them and names the other only after the first has closed. The filter stays on until the last one closes.

Order matters in three places here. The configuration is built before the rule table because the table's settings come from it. The rule table is built before either loader runs, because a loader classifying against an empty table gets the calendar's tagging and nothing else. Relevance is marked after whichever loader ran because it needs events in the array. Set
NewsFilterVerbose
to
true
on the first run. Each loader then prints every event it kept with its resolved tier and window, which is the quickest way to confirm the rules are matching what you expect.
Reading Your Own Broker
How your broker's calendar tags events, what strings it publishes as event codes, and what its server clock reads are facts about your terminal rather than facts about MQL5.
NewsTierInspector.mq5
reports all three. It is a script rather than an EA, and it includes
NewsRules.mqh
and nothing else. There is no
CTrade
instance in it and no position handling, which is possible because classification is now a question about data and can be answered without starting a trading system.
For each event in range at or above the
MinimumTier
input, the script prints the scheduled time, the currency, the broker's tier beside the resolved tier, the resolved window, the raw event code, and the name. Anything a rule moved is marked promoted or demoted with the index of the rule that moved it, and a summary counts them. The block below is not illustrative. for: The rule table is data-driven and loaded from a CSV file (NewsRules.csv), enabling editing without recompilation and allowing empirical testing of different event/window combinations.
The article explicitly states that the example minute values in NewsRules.csv 'are not measured figures' and instructs users to replace them with 'numbers you have tested on your own instrument'.
The classifier applies rules consistently to both live calendar data and historical CSV data, enabling identical logic to be verified in backtesting before live deployment.

The EA stores per-event windows (minutesBefore/minutesAfter) on the SNewsEvent record, allowing distinct time-based filters for different news types — a concrete, quantifiable parameter that can be optimized on historical data.

The built-in table contains 34 specific, named events (e.g., 'FOMC Press Conference', 'Nonfarm Payrolls') classified as NEWS_TIER_SPECIAL, each representing a testable hypothesis about prolonged market impact beyond standard high-impact news.

non_fatal: No explicit trading rule (entry condition) is provided — the article describes only a news filter that blocks or suspends trades around economic events, but does not define *when to enter* a trade (e.g., reversal after spike, breakout after consolidation, etc.).

No market-based feature or filter computable from price/spread/tick volume/time on closed bars is defined — all logic depends on external, non-market data: broker-provided economic calendar event names, codes, currencies, and timestamps.

The described mechanism requires access to the MQL5 Economic Calendar API (MqlCalendarEvent), which is not available for spot forex brokers without integrated economic calendar support; many retail forex brokers do not expose this API or provide incomplete/unaligned event data.
Relies on broker-specific event naming, translation, and event_code values — these are not standardized across brokers and cannot be reliably computed from OHLC/tick data.
No out-of-sample validation, spread modelling, or slippage considerations are included — but per instructions, these are non-fatal.

judge.reject_reason: Статья описывает фильтр экономических новостей на основе внешних данных из календаря (названия событий, коды, валюты, тайминги), а не торговое правило или рыночный признак, вычисляемый по ценам, спреду, тиковому объёму или времени по закрытым барам. Все ключевые элементы — event name, event_code, currency, importance — являются нерыночными, внешними, нестандартизированными и недоступными для большинства спот-форекс брокеров без интегрированного календаря. Отсутствует любая формула, зависящая от OHLC, времени бара, спреда или объёма. Это фильтр на основе макроэкономических метаданных, а не Strategy или Feature_Or_Filter в смысле задания.

repaint.note: Фильтр основан на событиях календаря с фиксированными временами — перерисовки нет, но это не рыночный признак.

higher_tf.note: Статья не использует старшие таймфреймы — она использует внешние события, не связанные с графиком.

tick_volume.note: Тиковый объём не упоминается и не используется.

judge.summary: Статья представляет собой реализацию фильтра торговых решений на основе экономического календаря MQL5, который классифицирует события по важности и назначает индивидуальные временные окна блокировки. Она не содержит ни торгового правила входа, ни рыночного признака, вычисляемого по ценовым данным или объёму — вся логика основана исключительно на внешних, нерыночных метаданных (названиях событий, кодах, валютах, таймингах).
